3.text: pole touches the ground. The short end is supported by a sweep, which

4.text: rests on a stake firmly set into the ground. One of the ends of the sweep

5.text: is connected by a willow withe or by a strong sinew cord with a trigger in

6.text: the middle of the fence. This trigger is held in place by a short wooden

7.text: stick, to which the bait is so tied that the first strong pull of the animal sets

8.text: the trigger free, and the roof, loosened from its support, falls heavily down

9.text: and crushes it (Fig. 50). For bait a dried salmon-head is used, or the wing-

10.text: bone of a goose, or something of that kind, usually in the most putrid state,

11.text: to attract the animals by its pungent smell.

12.text: On the tundra, dead-falls are often raised on special supports to prevent them

13.text: from being blocked by snowstorms. They are of slight build, being intended

14.text: chiefly for white foxes, and usually have two dropping-beams. Those within

15.text: the forest border, being intended for red foxes, are more strongly built, and

16.text: have three dropping-beams. However, the larger animals, such as wolverines

17.text: and wolves, are caught in them only when the flooring is made with spaces

18.text: between the poles. Then the feet of the animal will slip through, and the

19.text: sudden pain and pressure on its back will deprive it of most of its strength.

20.text: For hares a lighter dead-fall is used. It has only one stout beam; and the

21.text: fence is made simply of small stakes stuck in a row around the fall. Pieces

22.text: of willow-bark, or a few tender sprigs of willow or poplar, serve as bait, and
